title: The compiler back end: bytecode, native code and runtime parameters
body: After type checking, the compiler lowers the typedtree to *lambda*, a small untyped intermediate language in which pattern matches are already compiled to tests. From lambda, `ocamlc` produces portable *bytecode* that the `ocamlrun` interpreter executes, while `ocamlopt` goes on to produce native machine code (`-S` keeps the assembly). Both read the same source, and for a correct program they give the same output; native code is faster, bytecode is more portable and easier to debug.

`-dlambda` prints the lambda form, where a call in tail position is marked `tailcall`. Tail calls matter because the compiler turns a self tail call into a jump, so a tail-recursive loop uses constant stack space. The attribute `[@tailcall]` on a call asks the compiler to check this: with `-w +51` the compiler warns, and with `-warn-error +51` refuses to build, if the call is not actually a tail call. That makes the guarantee a compile-time check instead of a hope.

The runtime is configured without recompiling, through the `OCAMLRUNPARAM` environment variable. The setting `v=0x400` prints garbage-collection statistics when the program exits, `b` turns on backtraces, and `s` sets the minor heap size. Use these to see what the collector is doing before you decide whether any tuning is needed.
challenge: example/loop.ml marks a non-tail call with `[@tailcall]`, so the compiler rejects it under `-w +51 -warn-error +51`. Rewrite `sum` with an accumulator so the recursive call really is a tail call, keeping `Loop.sum 1_000_000 = 500000500000`.
projectInstructions: Try `ocamlfind ocamlopt -w +51 -warn-error +51 -c example/loop.ml`. Once it compiles, build both versions with `ocamlfind ocamlc -I example -o prog.byte example/loop.ml example/main.ml` and `ocamlfind ocamlopt -I example -o prog.exe example/loop.ml example/main.ml` (the `-I example` tells the compiler where to find `loop.cmi`), run them, and add `-dlambda` to see the tail call. Edit only example/loop.ml.
question: What does `[@tailcall]` with warning 51 enabled guarantee?
correct: That the marked call is in tail position, or compilation fails
wrong: That the function will be inlined
That the function runs on a second thread
reasoning: The attribute states an expectation and the warning checks it, so a refactoring that breaks tail-recursion is caught at compile time.

solution: the real tail call is accepted
